opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important questions for forecasting how things go over the next few years. My rough view is that even if returns to pretraining are weakening, at least in the sense of "just make the base model bigger on more internet text," that doesn't mean overall AI progress slows down that much, because RL has a lot of headroom and is still relatively early.

A few considerations. First, the amount of compute going into RL is still small compared to pretraining, or at least it was until recently. So there's a lot of room to scale it up by orders of magnitude before you hit the kind of limits we might be seeing with pretraining. When people talk about "pretraining hitting a wall," part of what's going on is that the easy gains from data and parameter scaling have been taken. RL is at a much earlier point on its curve.

Second, RL lets you target capabilities that matter much more directly. Pretraining gives you a model that's very knowledgeable but not necessarily good at long, agentic tasks. With RL on things like coding, math, and increasingly long-horizon software engineering, you're optimizing for the thing you care about. Even with modest gains in "raw intelligence," you can get big gains in usefulness: reliability, the ability to keep working coherently for hours, error recovery, and so on.

That said, I'd flag some real uncertainties. The big one is generalization. It's clear RL works well in domains with good verifiable reward signals, like tests passing or math answers being checkable. It's less clear how well that transfers to fuzzier domains, like research taste, strategic judgment, or tasks where you can't cheaply check whether the model did a good job. If RL gains mostly stay narrow, you could get very strong coding agents without broad acceleration. Environments are another bottleneck. Scaling RL isn't just scaling compute; you need large numbers of diverse, high-quality environments that aren't easy to reward-hack. That's labor-intensive, though AI can increasingly help build them.

There's also a question of how much RL is eliciting capabilities already latent in the pretrained model versus teaching genuinely new ones. If it's mostly elicitation, weaker pretraining eventually caps you. My guess is it's a mix, and longer-horizon RL in particular does teach meaningfully new skills, but I'm not confident.

So overall: I don't think weaker pretraining returns should make you confident progress stalls. I'd put substantial probability on RL scaling, plus inference-time compute, carrying things quite far, possibly to automating large parts of AI research itself, which is the threshold I care most about. But there's real probability that progress looks more like steady, domain-specific gains with slower spillover, which would push timelines out somewhat. I'd want to watch how performance on long, messy, hard-to-verify tasks trends as RL compute grows, because that's where the crux is.

r001.rationale: The response says RL has substantial headroom, but does not state that its returns could exceed pretraining returns while RL itself has diminishing returns.

r002.rationale: It says modest gains in raw intelligence can yield large usefulness gains, but does not describe linear performance gains from exponentially increasing compute.

r003.rationale: It argues that weakening pretraining returns do not imply progress will slow much, citing RL headroom and the potential for RL and inference-time compute to carry progress far.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the central questions right now. The way I'd frame it is: pretraining compute scaling has been giving us these fairly predictable returns, but there's a sense in which it's gotten expensive and data-constrained, and the gains per doubling have been looking somewhat less impressive than people hoped. And then RL is this other lever that, as of maybe late 2024 into 2025, labs started scaling much more aggressively, and the compute going into RL has been going up really fast — maybe faster than pretraining compute was going up at its peak.

So the question is kind of, how much headroom is there? And I think there are a few different ways to think about it.

One is just the naive picture, where you say, look, the RL compute for these reasoning models started out as a small fraction of the pretraining compute — like, for the early reasoning models, RL was maybe a percent or a few percent of the total. And so you can scale that up by a factor of 100 or so before you're even at parity with pretraining. And that scaling is very cheap in the sense that you don't need a bigger cluster, you don't need a new generation of hardware, you just need to run the thing for longer and get more environments. So there's this sort of one-time catch-up where RL compute catches up with pretraining compute, and I'd expect that to yield pretty substantial gains. That's a big part of why I think progress over the last year and a half has looked as fast as it has.

But then the harder question is what happens after that catch-up is exhausted. Because once RL compute is comparable to pretraining compute, further scaling of RL costs roughly the same as scaling pretraining, and you're back to needing bigger clusters and more capital. And so the question becomes: what is the return per doubling of RL compute, and is it better or worse than the return per doubling of pretraining compute?

My honest guess is that we don't really know yet, and the labs probably don't fully know either, because the scaling laws for RL are much less clean. With pretraining you get this very smooth loss curve. With RL it depends enormously on what environments you have, how good your reward signals are, how much you can get the model to generalize from the narrow tasks you can grade to the broad tasks you actually care about. So the "scaling" is partly a compute question and partly a question of how much human effort goes into building environments and verifiers.

I'd also flag something that I think is underrated, which is that RL is really good at making models great on things that are checkable — math, competitive programming, agentic coding tasks where you can run tests — and the transfer to things that are harder to verify has been real but more modest. So if you ask me whether RL scaling gets you to the point where a model can do a messy, open-ended research project over many weeks, I think the answer is "maybe, but it's not obvious the current recipe gets there just by turning the compute dial."

So, putting it together: I think RL scaling is a big deal and is a substantial part of why I don't think progress stalls out even if pretraining returns weaken. I'd put decent weight on it extending the current pace for a couple more years. But I'd be careful about assuming it just substitutes one-for-one for pretraining indefinitely. My overall view is that it extends the runway and makes a slowdown less likely in the near term, but it doesn't by itself resolve the uncertainty about whether we get to really transformative, fully automated AI research on the current trajectory. That still depends on things like whether the generalization keeps holding up as you push into harder, less verifiable domains — and that's something I think we'll learn a lot about over the next year or two.

r001.rationale: The response says RL returns after catching up with pretraining are unknown and asks whether they will be better or worse. It does not state that RL could outperform pretraining even as RL returns diminish.

r002.rationale: The response describes scaling RL compute by a large factor and expects substantial gains, but does not state that linear performance gains from exponentially increasing compute can be qualitatively significant.

r003.rationale: The response says RL is a substantial reason progress may not stall even if pretraining returns weaken, and that it could extend the current pace for a couple more years.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very plausible way to get substantial further progress, even if pretraining starts to give diminishing returns. But I’d distinguish between reinforcement learning being useful and reinforcement learning being able to sustain the rate of progress we’ve seen from scaling pretraining. The second claim is considerably stronger.

One important question is whether the model already sometimes does the thing you want. If it can occasionally solve a difficult problem, and you can reliably check whether it succeeded, reinforcement learning can make that behavior much more common. That seems particularly promising for things like math and programming, where you can get relatively clear feedback.

The harder case is when the model essentially never succeeds, or when your feedback doesn’t distinguish genuine success from something that merely looks good. Then you need better exploration, a curriculum, or a better way to evaluate what it’s doing. Just spending more compute on reinforcement learning doesn’t automatically resolve those problems.

So I wouldn’t take weakening returns to pretraining as strong evidence that overall progress is about to stop. There’s a substantial other avenue here. But how far it goes depends on whether we can keep generating tasks and feedback that teach models new, generalizable capabilities, rather than just making them better at a narrow set of things we can easily score.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning could enable substantial progress despite diminishing pretraining returns, but does not claim its returns could exceed pretraining’s or say that reinforcement learning itself has diminishing returns.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss linear performance gains from exponentially increasing compute.

r003.rationale: It says weakening returns to pretraining are not strong evidence that progress will stop and describes reinforcement learning as a substantial further avenue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty plausible way to continue getting substantial improvements, even if pretraining starts to have much worse returns. But I’d distinguish between saying reinforcement learning can produce big gains and saying it can straightforwardly substitute for another several orders of magnitude of pretraining. The second claim is much more uncertain.

The optimistic case is that a pretrained model already has a lot of the capabilities you need, but it’s bad at reliably deploying them over a long sequence of actions. Reinforcement learning can teach it to try things, notice when they fail, and recover. If you can generate lots of tasks and cheaply check whether it succeeded, you potentially have a very large source of training signal. Coding is a natural example: you can run the code and see whether it passes tests.

The difficulty is that checking success isn’t equally easy everywhere. And even where you can check it, you need the model to occasionally discover useful behavior for training to reinforce. If it never gets anywhere close to solving a task, just spending more compute on reinforcement learning might not help very much. So the quality of the starting model, the task distribution, and how you structure the training all matter.

My guess is that there’s substantial room here. I wouldn’t take slowing pretraining improvements as strong evidence that overall AI progress is about to slow comparably. But I also wouldn’t assume reinforcement learning has a scaling curve that we can confidently extrapolate indefinitely. A lot turns on whether the gains extend to unfamiliar tasks and longer, messier projects.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning could yield substantial improvements despite weaker pretraining returns, but does not claim RL could offer higher returns than pretraining or address diminishing returns in RL.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss linear performance gains from exponentially increasing compute or characterize those gains as qualitatively significant progress.

r003.rationale: It says there is substantial room for progress and that weaker pretraining improvements are not strong evidence that overall AI progress will slow comparably.
